piece.caption:
How to protect business accounting data from public AI model training leaks. Pasting supplier ledgers, customer GST numbers, and profit margins into free AI chat tools can expose your underlying data to public model training. MeitY's new DEPA architecture requires confidential clean rooms and differential privacy so raw datasets remain inaccessible. Standard AI chat windows do not provide these institutional safeguards by default. Always sanitize sensitive numbers before prompting.

Comment DATA for the breakdown of official AI data protection standards.

piece.dm_text:
MeitY ke proposed DEPA framework ke mutabiq, AI training ke dauran sensitive data protect karne ke technical pillars:

1. Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments jahan data processing hoti hai bina underlying dataset expose kiye.
2. Differential Privacy: Aisi privacy technique jisse individual-level information identify ya extract nahi ho sakti.
3. Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements jo data-sharing conditions aur security enforce karte hain.
4. Zero-Trust Security: Har access request authenticate aur encrypt hoti hai continuous monitoring ke sath.

Standard chatbots mein raw customer GST, turnover aur margins direct paste mat karein.

issues: The reel conflates two different concepts: OpenAI's robots.txt update (which is about web crawling) and the MeitY DEPA framework (which is about data sharing for AI training). While both relate to data privacy, they are distinct mechanisms. The current flow might confuse a user into thinking they are the same thing.

The transition between the 'Public AI' risk and the 'DEPA' solution needs to be clearer so the viewer understands DEPA is a government-proposed framework for the future, not a feature currently available in ChatGPT.
review.fix_instructions: Add a brief clarifying sentence in the narration or a small on-screen text note in Scene 3 to distinguish that the DEPA framework is a government-proposed architecture for secure data sharing, distinct from the standard settings in public chatbots. Otherwise, the content is excellent and highly relevant for the target audience.

[40] OpenAI News — Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
URL: https://openai.com/index/helping-websites-express-ai-training-preferences
Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences | OpenAI OpenAI October 30, 2026
Why we’re supporting a common signal that lets website operators communicate their choices to multiple AI providers at once.
Share Today, we’re announcing that OpenAI will honor a common signal ⁠ (opens in a new window) in robots.txt, the file that lets websites express their preferences about the use of their content for foundational generative AI training. This voluntary effort makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.
Previously, website operators would identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider. Having a shared signal across multiple providers reduces that work for operators.
We aim to implement the signal in the coming months, and will share another update with details about our implementation when we do so. This new signal will not replace the controls we already provide through robots.txt. Our existing crawler controls ⁠ (opens in a new window) , which provide web publishers flexibility and control over their pages, will continue to apply and be respected.
This draws on the ongoing work ⁠ (opens in a new window) of the Internet Engineering Task Force’s (IETF) AI Preferences working group. We’re joining other participants in the working group in today’s announcement of this shared signal, and believe this strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions. OpenAI will continue to adapt its practices as those conversations and the landscape continue to evolve in view of appropriate controls and fairness.
We believe this is a practical step toward an open web where people can publish and discover information, and website owners have clearer, simpler ways to communicate their choices about how their content is used. We encourage other AI providers to honor the signal.

The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India.
Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens’ privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act.
The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets.
With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT.
The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars:
Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another
Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset
Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements
Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data
The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models:
Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies
Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models
Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants
Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability.
TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access.
Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers.
The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling.
Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training.
The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27.
As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines . The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology.
A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation .
